data.title: The Kiev Missal – the oldest Old Church Slavonic manuscript
data.excerpt: The Kiev Missal consists of 7 parchment folios written in the oldest surviving type of Glagolitic script and contains 38 short prayers. Its dating is uncertain, roughly the end of the 9th to the beginning of the 10th century, and scholars still disagree whether it is a copy of a Great Moravian original or the original itself.
data.metaTitle: The Kiev Missal – the oldest Old Church Slavonic manuscript
data.metaDescription: The Kiev Missal: 7 parchment folios in the oldest Glagolitic uncial, 38 short prayers, and the still-open dispute over its Great Moravian origin.

children.text: Language:
Old Church Slavonic
Script:
Glagolitic uncial, the oldest surviving type
Dating:
uncertain, probably the end of the 9th to the beginning of the 10th century
Place of deposit:
the library of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences
Place of discovery:
the Sinai Peninsula, probably St Catherine's Monastery (the finder did not state the place of discovery)
Finder:
Archimandrite Antonin, Andrei Ivanovich Kapustin, * 12 August 1817 Baturino, Perm – † 24 March 1894, Jerusalem

The Kiev Missal consists of 7 parchment folios measuring 15 cm × 11.5 cm. The script suggests that several scribes wrote it. The first, opening page 1r was added later, in a younger period. The pages that follow are linguistically older than the first page and are written in a different form of Glagolitic. Moreover, folios 1v–2v up to the seventh line were written by a different hand than the remaining pages. The Kiev Missal has an archaic language and the oldest surviving type of Glagolitic.
The contents of the Kiev Missal

In all they contain 38 short prayers. The opening page 1r is younger; a part of the Apostle Paul's Epistle to the Romans and a prayer to Mary were added to the blank folio later. The older folios 1v–7v contain a mass for St Clement, followed by a mass for St Felicitas, whose feast falls on the same day, six masses for each day and two votive masses: for the martyrs and for all the heavenly powers.
A copy or the original

It is regarded as the first copy of a Glagolitic original of Great Moravian origin. Views also appear that it could have been written directly in the Great Moravian period. Radoslav Večerka described the Kiev Missal as a “representative of Old Church Slavonic of the Great Moravian type” and, in agreement with F. V. Mareš, regards it directly as the original from the Cyrillo-Methodian school, produced probably in Rome at the end of 868.1 The manuscript is still not precisely dated.
The discovery, story one: Archimandrite Antonin

In 1865 Father Antonin was sent to lead the mission to Jerusalem. He left Athens reluctantly, the mission where he had served since completing his studies at the Kiev Theological Academy. In Athens, besides his own mission, he was actively engaged in archaeological research, in the palaeography of religious inscriptions in churches and in the development of the Greek language. He published the results and is the author of numerous studies. In Jerusalem he devoted considerable attention to old manuscripts and to church history. He promoted religious tolerance and, in keeping with his missionary work, had several schools built. His diary has survived, in which he described his activity from August 1830 to January 1894, and also a detailed description of the library of precious manuscripts of St Catherine's Monastery on Sinai. Before his death he visited the Russian consul general in Jerusalem, Sergei Vasilievich Arsenev, in order to arrange the transport of a part of the items he had acquired during his life to various institutions in Russia. In this way the 7 parchment folios came to the Kiev Theological Academy. On the upper side of the Kiev Missal there is an inscription in Russian: “To the library of the Kiev Theological Academy, Jerusalem, 2 May 1872.” It is assumed that this is the handwriting of Father Antonin. 2
A new discovery, story two: St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, Egypt

On 25 May 1975 Archimandrite Sophronius was supervising reconstruction work in the rubble of an old, partly collapsed tower of the northern wall of the monastery. The workmen had to break through one wall and unexpectedly discovered a small room, and in it a chest full of damaged manuscripts in several languages: Greek, Arabic, Syriac, Hebrew, Latin, Ethiopic and Slavonic. The oldest Greek one was from the 4th century AD; another manuscript, written in Caucasian Albanian, is the only one preserved in that language at all; parts of a manuscript of Homer's Iliad from the 9th century were found, as well as parchments written in Glagolitic. It turned out that the room had been used for centuries as a store of old manuscripts. At the beginning of the 19th century the manuscripts were moved to the new monastery library and the damaged ones remained in the chest. The Sinai Peninsula was subsequently struck by an earthquake, the ceiling of the small room collapsed and the chest remained forgotten. 3
Story three: Demetrius

The unknown damaged Glagolitic manuscripts found in 1975 were photographed on Sinai in 2007 using the technology of the Austrian Academy of Sciences and were examined by the team of Heinz Miklas from the University of Vienna. A connection between the texts and the Kiev Missal emerged. The same hand wrote the opening page of the Kiev Missal as well as the Sinai manuscripts designated Sin. Slav. 3/N and Sin. Slav. 5/N. The same person also wrote in Cyrillic and in Greek in these documents. The codex Sin. Slav. 3/N gives the name Demetrius, and the manuscript was given the title Psalterium Demetrii Sinaitici. The opening page of the Kiev Missal, added later, thus acquired an author. Demetrius also wrote the codex designated Sin. Slav. 5/N, and it contains a prayer concerning Aligernus. If this is Aligernus, the abbot of Montecassino, he died in 986. Demetrius therefore could not have written the codex before that year. 4,5
Linguistics

The Old Church Slavonic language was used over a wider territory, not only in Great Moravia, and also for a long time after the expulsion of Methodius's disciples. Old Church Slavonic and the Glagolitic script were used, for example, by the Czech monastery of Sázava, as well as by the monasteries of the Bulgarian-Macedonian region and the scribal school at the monastery of Ohrid. One of the tasks of Slavic studies, or palaeoslavistics, is to find such words or grammar as were used only in the territory of Great Moravia and nowhere else. If a manuscript contains them, it would be proof that it was written in Great Moravia, if only… If only copying were not the sole means of disseminating books. A codex with the language of Great Moravia may be merely an exact copy several centuries younger. There are many speculations, but present-day linguistics agrees on the following. The features indicating the Great Moravian origin of the exemplar of the Kiev Missal are:

1. the Great Moravian cultural sphere used “šč” in the place where the rest of the Old Church Slavonic sphere used “št”. For example, the words “zaščiti, očiščenie” recorded in the Kiev Missal are Great Moravian, while Old Church Slavonic manuscripts used “zaštiti”.

2. the form of the word “cirЪky” with “cir” belongs only to the language of the Slavs in Great Moravia. In Old Church Slavonic the form is “crЬky”. This form with “i” is widespread in Kajkavian Croatian, in eastern Slovenian and in Old Polish. Old Czech had the form ciérkev.
3. the form of the instrumental singular masculine ending in “ЪmЬ” also belongs to Great Moravia. For example “nadЪ oplatЪmЬ”
Likewise the instrumental singular feminine ending in “ojǫ”. For example: silojo̧, slavojo̧.6

4. Besides those mentioned above, Radoslav Večerka considers the following to be Great Moravianisms: the precise observance of the use of the jers, and the preservation and distinction of the nasal vowels. He admits that it is hard to decide with certainty, but he considers the following words to be Great Moravian: rěsnota – truth, ašut – in vain, needlessly, inokostЬ – exile.
Palaeography

The Kiev Missal was written by several scribes and in different periods. The opening page 1r, originally blank, was added later; its author has been named Demetrius Sinaiticus. The pages that follow are older, but at least two scribes can be distinguished there as well. 1v–2v:7, i.e. the first page and the second page up to line 7, were written by scribe A, the rest by scribe B, both unknown. The folios contain many abbreviations and marks.

1. most often they abbreviated by contracting words (per contractionem), writing a line – a titlo – above the shortened word. For example: the word Bože was shortened to “bže”, the word gospodi to “gi”.

2. they abbreviated by means of the so-called ligature: part of the preceding letter forms part of the following letter. This abbreviation occurs on the opening page 1r (i.e. recto), which was added later. In the word “pomom” = let us pray. The letter L is written above the word and is joined to the letter M.

Marks in the Kiev Missal: they are not used consistently even within a single page. On the first page (1verso), in the first prayer, the scribe separated sentences with a colon and the end of a paragraph with five dots. On the same page, but in the second prayer, he separated sentences with a single dot and paragraphs with a colon. Because this marking is quite different in other Glagolitic manuscripts, it may be a sign of different scribal schools.
Numbers: these were separated from the text by a dot before and after the number and at the same time by a stroke above the number.
The breathings here have two graphic marks, ¬ and its inverted version; they were written above vowels and indicated soft pronunciation.7
Liturgical typology

The Kiev Missal is a self-contained work, not merely a fragment = an incomplete part of an originally longer manuscript, as the first studies assumed.8 Liturgical typology investigates which rite was used in Great Moravia, the Eastern Greek or the Western Roman one. How exactly did the liturgy proceed in Great Moravia? The written records say first the Roman rite, then the Slavonic one. That remains the only reliable fact, and the view is held that the schism of the churches in the times of Great Moravia was not as acute as it was a few centuries later.

A sacramentary is the technical term for a Roman mass book, a euchologion for a Greek mass book. The mass books were compared with the Kiev Missal, and the results show that the most similar texts were those of the sacramentaries in the Salzburg diocese and the Patriarchate of Aquileia in the 9th century. The most similar one, Paduanus D47, agrees with the Kiev Missal to about 80%.

Further comparisons were made with the so-called libelli missae. Libelli missae are a selection for masses from various sacramentaries, gospel books, apostle books and other prayers, at the discretion of individual missionaries. The comparison showed that the libelli missae found so far (the Stowe Missal of Irish origin, Codex 1395 from St Gallen) are from the 7th–8th centuries and were used by missionaries in the spread of Christianity. They are therefore too old and come from places too distant, and no certain connection with the Kiev Missal was found. Above all, these libelli selections were made so that a single mass book would suffice for missionaries when celebrating mass. The Kiev Missal could not be used as an independent mass book, since the canon of the mass is missing, and so a further manuscript was needed. The Kiev Missal does not contain the text needed for the celebration of the most important feasts, and it could not be used during the seasons of Advent and Easter. So much for the earliest period of the use of the Kiev Missal. We shall skip a century or so (because the precise dating is not yet available) and the Kiev Missal came, in a way so far unknown, into the hands of a man named Demetrius Sinaiticus. Because the Kiev Missal could not be used on its own, he added a suitable text to the blank opening page. Ľ. Lukovíny compared the manuscript Sin. Slav. 5/N written by Demetrius, the Psalterium Demetrii, the Euchologium Sinaiticum and the Kiev Missal as supplemented by Demetrius. On the opening page of the Kiev Missal a reading from St Paul to the Romans has been added, which is used in Greek texts at the beginning of the Lenten and Easter season. Demetrius combined sacramentary texts (i.e. texts of the Roman rite) according to the system of the euchologion (that is, according to the mass of the Greek rite). In this period, that is at the end of the 10th and the beginning of the 11th century, the Old Church Slavonic mass was probably celebrated neither according to the euchologion nor according to the sacramentary, but precisely by the combination of both of these liturgical books (sacralogion).
Prayer no. 20

The use of Old Church Slavonic in the liturgy made it necessary to translate the basic church books into this language. The Kiev Missal is also a translation, but prayer no. 20 differs greatly from its Latin exemplar. And here too the prevailing agreement is that we do not agree.

Eugen Paulíny: “No Latin exemplar for it has been found at all; it might be regarded as an original work. But this is contradicted by the numerous Latinisms accumulated in this short text....This prayer, too, is therefore translated from Latin”. Slovesnosť a kultúrny jazyk Veľkej Moravy (Literary Art and the Cultural Language of Great Moravia), 1964.

Josef Vašica: “ In prayer no. 20 the only point of contact between the Latin exemplar and the Slavonic text is the first word Rege; it was on this that the author's idea caught hold”...Slovo a slovesnost 2, vol. 6, 1940. (In this article Vašica describes numerous Byzantine elements in the Kiev Missal and joins the theory that the folios were copied in a Czech milieu).

Ján Stanislav: “The procedure of the translator of the Latin original in the given text of prayer no. 20 is therefore in no way accidental but, on the contrary, historically justified”...Starosloviensky jazyk 1 (Old Church Slavonic 1), 1978.

Paulíny considered the Latin text so different that it could not have been the exemplar for prayer no. 20; Vašica, on the other hand, held that the author merely paraphrased the Latin text freely in verse. Ján Stanislav suggested that it is an original Great Moravian text inserted into the original Latin prayer out of fears of the penetration of smaller detachments of Hungarians into the Carpathian Basin.
The Kiev Missal and the Life of Constantine-Cyril

A comparison of prayer no. 20, for which there is no exact Latin exemplar, was also published by V. V. Nimchuk, who found a text with the same idea, and directly in a manuscript from the Great Moravian school. The Life of Constantine-Cyril is an extensive biographical work written by one of Constantine's disciples between 873 and 879. In it he recorded Constantine's prayer before death. “And when the hour drew near to receive rest and to move to the eternal dwellings, he raised his hands to God and prayed with tears and spoke thus....blessed is God, who did not give us up as prey to the teeth of our invisible enemies”...

In this prayer before death Nimchuk also pointed out a further agreement with the Kiev Missal. The Life of Constantine: “thou hast founded the earth and brought everything that exists from non-being into being”. In the Kiev Missal: “gi otЪ nebЪitia bo vЪ bЪitie sЪtvoril nЪi esi”.9,10
Conclusion
What we have not managed to track down, and what is therefore also missing from this survey, is any more extensive explanation of the words vЪlítije and a comparison of rov – rovanijȩ.

The Kiev Missal is generally regarded as a copy also because of the word rovanijȩ.11 Theories developed from the idea that the original manuscript had darovanijȩ. Later the word rovanijȩ was found in another manuscript. As an explanation, the theory appeared that the word comes from the Old High German word arvani. We have not found whether anyone has investigated a connection with the Slovak word rov, used in literary language in the sense of a burial mound, where a transferred meaning of the word might already be involved, if gifts were placed in pre-Christian burial mounds.
